title: Rick and Morty showrunners explain the reason for season 9's brutal finale
author: @xcomsamanthanelson1
content:
Follow

Link copied to clipboard

Published Jul 26, 2026, 11:00 PM EDT

‘There is a concern that the show becomes unrecognizable.’

Rick and Morty showrunners explain the reason for season 9's brutal finale

Sign in to your Polygon.com account

Morty Smith has been through a lot over the course of nine seasons of adventuring with his grandpa Rick Sanchez in Rick and Morty. He’s had his consciousness fragmented into a video game’s NPCs, fled his own dimension, buried himself, and met his brilliant, evil doppelgänger. Season 8 ended with Morty facing his greatest fears, and the season 9 finale was another brutal episode that forced Morty to face some dark truths.

“If we stop putting him through [these situations], I guess there is a concern that the show becomes unrecognizable,” showrunner Dan Harmon told Polygon in a virtual interview. “Morty has been a 14-year-old boy for over a decade, and that decade has subjected him to hourly life trauma and a relationship with one of the most abusive people in the universe.”

[Ed. note: This article contains spoilers for the Rick and Morty season 9 finale]

“Field of Dreams” opens with a bunch of versions of Rick (Ian Cardoni) and Morty (Harry Belden) visiting an estate sale at the home of a Smith family who died from eating chili so spicy it made their intestines explode. Morty meets a version of himself that likes to “funeral hop” to hear versions of his family say nice things about him and decides to give it a try. He eventually finds a version of his family that has never met another Morty before.

They seem like the ideal family, showering him with love and offering him the chance to visit them whenever he wants, and they’re shocked by the tales of what he’s been through on his adventures with Rick. But eventually Morty sees their dark side as Jerry (Chris Parnell) breaks the portal gun to keep him from going back to his own world.

The reason this version of the Smith family is so different is that they broke off all contact with Rick because he refused to address his alcoholism. Morty tracks down Rick and discovers one of the healthiest versions of Rick we’ve ever seen. He’s been sober for 17 years, is happily married, and teaches at MIT. Rick acknowledges that the quest to invent a portal gun nearly ruined his life, but Morty pushes him to do it anyway. The obsession ruins his marriage and drives him back to drinking and nihilism, turning him into the Rick that Morty has always known.

By the end of the episode, Morty’s back to adventuring with a drunk, irresponsible Rick. Co-showrunner Scott Marder told Polygon that the dysfunctional dynamic between the two characters is “kind of the heart of the show.”

“The finale actually examines it in a really cool way that Morty’s been corrupted by this relationship in a lot of ways, but he’s basically forced to corrupt Rick to get what he wants, which was a cool full circle thing for him at the end of season 9.”

While Morty hasn’t aged during the show’s nine seasons, he has been changed by his brutal adventures.

“I think we have organically grown Morty while still keeping the core of his identity,” Harmon said. “He’s an idealist. He believes in truth. He believes that there is a right way to do things. At the core, Rick has grown too, but he doesn’t really believe that. Their growth occurs while keeping the characters real.”

title: Is [redacted] really dead after House of the Dragon season 3 episode 6?
author: @xcomCoreyIsAFox
content:
Follow

Link copied to clipboard

Published Jul 26, 2026, 10:00 PM EDT

This one character cheated death before — can they do it again?

House of the Dragon leaves one character's fate hanging by a thread

Sign in to your Polygon.com account

Aside from some major deaths, some of the toughest drama to watch in House of the Dragon season 3 has everything to do with the fabled Sea Snake, Corlys Velaryon (Steve Toussaint), reckoning with his life and legacy. After his wife, Princess Rhaenys Targaryen (Eva Best), died at the Battle of Rook’s Rest in season 2, something in Corlys changed. He acknowledged that Alyn and Addam were his sons, and especially after his near-death experience in the Battle of the Gullet — during which his castle, High Tide, was ransacked — Corlys looked to the future even more. After Rhaenyra Targaryen (Emma D’Arcy) successfully took over King’s Landing and claimed the Iron Throne, he pleaded with her to legitimize Alyn (Abubakar Salim) and Addam (Clinton Liberty) as his rightful heirs. Yet she refused.

That tension simmers in season 3 episode 6, and it ultimately makes what happens at the very end of the episode so difficult to watch.

[Ed. note: Spoilers follow for House of the Dragon season 3 episode 6 and the source material Fire & Blood.]

Episode 6 feels like one of those classic Game of Thrones episodes where a lot of little things happen to slowly inch various plotlines forward. There aren’t any enormous battles, dragon fights, or even shouting matches. The show feels rather spread out across its various characters and subplots. One of the few spectacles happens early in the episode when Ser Criston Cole (Fabien Frankel) stands ready to fight to the death against Team Black’s army only for him to be unceremoniously peppered with arrows from a distance. It’s as satisfying for the viewer as it was unsatisfying for Cole himself. The rest of the episode is a lot of simmering tension as the plot inches forward.

In King’s Landing, Alyn of Hull is coming into his own as the de facto Hand of the King. Episode 5 explored how a mystery group of people loyal to Team Green — specifically Daeron’s claim to the throne as puppeted by Ormund Hightower (James Norton) — and now gold cloaks have resigned en masse. Alyn comes up with a solution: leverage Velaryon troops in King’s Landing to serve as the temporary city watch. She requests that he petition Corlys for more.

Alyn catches up with Corlys, who’s been fighting against repeated Triarchy raids, to put the request in. Corlys agrees but remains angry at the fact that Rhaenyra refuses to legitimize Addam and Alyn. “And how many years did it take you to do the same?” Alyn replies.

Toward the end of the episode, seemingly in direct response to Rhaenyra sending assassins to Tumbleton that posed as Baratheon soldiers, the queen receives a message that reads, “Kick this dog and it will bite your hand.” Then the episode cuts to Corlys’ camp. He delivers an impassioned speech to his soldiers in which he admits that he’s been gone from the city for too long.

Afterward, he turns and sees a stranger (who is one of Ormund's personal guards), before he’s quickly grabbed from behind and seemingly strangled. The moment is left deliberately ambiguous — doubly so because nothing like this sequence of events is presented in Fire & Blood. Is this the end of Corlys Velaryon?

Is Corlys Velaryon dead?

Given the fact that Fire & Blood is presented as a maester aggregating various historical accounts of the Dance of Dragons, concrete details about private conversations and secret assassinations are scarce. As such, House of the Dragon consistently takes a lot of liberties to flesh out those finer details.

It’s certainly possible that Corlys Velaryon dies here, but unlike Cole who takes an arrow to the face, we never actually see Corlys clearly getting stabbed. After he’s grabbed from behind, the camera cuts to a wide shot far behind him as he seemingly struggles against his attackers. Other assassins swarm the woods around them, attacking his troops. Corlys has already survived what looked like certain death once this season, and he seems destined to do so again.

The fact is, Corlys still has a very important role to play in the events of the civil war moving forward. Our best guess is that no, Corlys is not dead. He’s merely been captured by assassins sent by Ormund Hightower. The Dance with Dragons takes a major turn following the impending battle at Tumbleton, and Corlys maintains an important political figure through the rest of the war. If he were to die now, it would mark the single biggest deviation from the books that the show has taken yet. Which is to say that you can likely consider Corlys safe — for now.

House of the Dragon airs weekly at 9 p.m. Eastern on HBO and HBO Max.

title: Nobody remembers the most inventive vampire thriller of the 2000s, but it's free to stream right now
author: Maria Loreto
content:
Follow

Link copied to clipboard

Published Jul 26, 2026, 8:00 PM EDT

Bring back cheesy vampire movies

The 2000s were a great time for cheesy vampire movies. Shortly before the Twilight franchise turned bloodsuckers into tortured romantic heroes for young adults, countless vampire flicks were released, filled with cringy dialogue and shlocky action sequences. Films like Van Helsing and Queen of the Damned aren’t the sharpest of what the genre can offer, but contain amazing moments of vampire lore, like an eerie masquerade ball depicting vampires without their reflection, or an undead rockstar climbing the walls to terrorize his groupies.

One of the most innovative movies of that era is Daybreakers, which took the cheesy vampire subgenre and transformed it into a dystopian sci-fi thriller. Written and directed by twin brothers Michael and Peter Spierig, this 2010 movie stars Ethan Hawke, Willem Dafoe, and the late Sam Neill, and is streaming for free on Pluto TV. It’s the rare example of a movie that fully embraces the joys of the vampire genre and is unafraid to be ridiculous or excessive while trying out something completely new.

Daybreakers takes place in an alternate and dystopian future of (get ready for it) 2019. Vampires are the dominant species and the remaining enslaved humans are about to go extinct, meaning the main source of food/blood is about to disappear. Hawke plays Edward, a vampire hematologist who doesn’t drink human blood and is developing an alternate food source that will allow vampires to live without harming others. This will also prevent the rise of the Subsiders, a monstrous breed of the undead that starving vampires have begun transforming into. These creatures are rabid and bat-like, sprouting large wings from their backs and huge fangs that deform their faces.

To develop the Subsider design, the filmmakers turned to practical effects, with performers wearing full-body foam latex suits that almost look like Orcs from The Lord of the Rings.

“When people see the Subsiders, I wanted them to feel pity and disgust before they felt fear,” the movie’s creature designer, Steven Boyle, told the Los Angeles Times in 2010. “The foam latex has a faint sulfur smell,” continued Boyle. “And the glues are alcohol-based. So, by the end of the day, it’s a lovely human stew of sulfur, sweat, talcum powder and KY jelly.”

That hard, sweaty work paid off, and the look of the creatures remains one of the film’s highlights, even 17 years later.

Beyond its practical effects, Daybreakers hinges on a complicated and self-serious plot, yet one that is still incredibly fun. The first quarter of the film is centered on Edward’s life and his job conducting gory tests on his human subjects. He's micromanaged by his boss, Charles (Sam Neill), a vampire CEO who doesn’t share his humanistic tendencies. His life is derailed after a chance encounter with a group of rebels led by Lionel (Willem Dafoe), a human who used to be a vampire and was miraculously transformed back to his original self, putting them on a dangerous hunt to find a cure for vampirism and spark some hope for the future of humanity.

Daybreakers could have been another generic action thriller in the hands of other filmmakers, but the Spiering brothers were fully committed to their depiction of a dark and brooding vampire dystopia. The characters all wear old-fashioned suits and dresses despite the twisted modernity that surrounds them, whether that’s in their grand and sterile homes or at their office jobs in high-rise buildings. Throughout the film, these clinical spaces are interrupted by bursts of nature, with the filmmakers lingering on wide establishing shots of beautiful landscapes, desolate roads and vast deserts.

And despite its far-out concept and plot-heavy script, Daybreakers still pays great attention to the practicalities of being a vampire. Edward is memorably introduced as an empty suit in a mirror’s reflection. His blacked-out car plays a great supporting character as he drives around town in the daytime, protected from sunlight, while allowing him to view the outside world through multiple screens.

Hawke's Edward is one in a string of truly committed performances highlighted in the film. The Oscar-nominated actor could have just taken the paycheck and phoned it in. Instead, he turns in a tortured dramatic performance on par with Before Sunrise. Dafoe appears sporadically but memorably, delivering cheesy one-liners with a straight face. Without spoiling things, the cure his group is seeking involves exposing vampires to the sun. Lionel’s response? “Fuck it, I love a good barbecue.” Neill is also a standout, unhinged and gleeful, covered in blood and rolling around on the floor in agony. It’s a reminder that he was the rare character actor who never took himself too seriously, and was down to try anything.

Daybreakers received mixed reviews upon its release but it has been rediscovered in recent years, becoming a modern cult classic. The movie is a rare example of a pair of filmmakers trying out something new within the constraints of an oversaturated genre, and a great reminder of the power of craft and practical effects. It’s unabashedly cheesy and campy, something that modern vampire movies could use more of.

Daybreakers is free to stream on Pluto TV.

title: The Sunday Papers
author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
content:
Read more

Sundays are for sobbingly lifting exactly one boulder from the groaning dreampile that is my backlog. Good news, Vacuity, cpt_freakout and the rest – I'm trying out your precious, precious Troubleshooter game. I hear it's a hundred hours long, so please do not take this as a promise that a write-up is forthcoming. So far my major takeaways are 1) I enjoy collecting masteries, aka packages of abilities and modifiers, and 2) this "Short Break" track is cooool. Please hum along while browsing our latest collection of Rollicking Reads.

For Aeon, Ali Rıza Taşkale analyses how self-appointed big tech visionaries have borrowed the trappings of Western sci-fi and fantasy works such as Neuromancer, the Foundation novels, and Star Trek for their political projects. I think you could get a whole 'nother essay out of this excerpt on how the threat of sci-fantasy apocalypse gets perversely deployed as a means of distraction.

It is the triumph of the speculative sci-fi scenario over human solidarity: why fix the world we inhabit when we can spend billions preventing a robot uprising that exists only in the imagination? By trying to steer policy debates toward distant catastrophic scenarios – killer robots, rogue AI, existential risk – the industry diverts attention from regulating the systems already causing harm: algorithmic bias in hiring, facial recognition’s racial disparities, platform amplification of extremism.

For the LRB, Jenny Turner writes about the Scottish novelist Lewis Grassic Gibbon (birthname James Leslie Mitchell), exploring nationalism, patriarchy, class, place, language, and changing times. I've never read any Gibbon/Mitchell, but I found this piece quite enveloping. It's a longer one – 10,000 words.

Scots is love, English learning, and you can’t do much of the latter before you lose your roots: it still runs deep, this Oedipal confusion of nation and class and agency and power, and without it, there’s no way [Nicola] Sturgeon’s vaguely social-democratic Scottish nationalism would ever have wrung and held the hearts of people the way it did. Much of it, as Sturgeon senses, has to do with ‘Scots words’, as instruments of interpellation really, especially when your heart is getting held and wrung by them at school. Gibbon’s use of Scots is quite confusing, an artefact that looks authentic although it’s not: ‘The technique,’ as he confessed, ‘is to mould the English language into the rhythms and cadences of Scots spoken speech, and to inject into the English vocabulary such minimum number of words from Braid Scots as that remodelling requires.’ He was keen for his book to sell, to American audiences in particular, and appended a glossary of around a hundred words to the American edition. The most used ‘Scotticisms’, according to William K. Malcolm’s new biography, are modifiers such as awful, bit, coarse, fair, fell, ‘cosmetic rather than descriptive’, easy enough for diaspora Scots, more than a quarter of a million of whom left for North America in the 1920s alone.

For Stop Caring, an anonymous writer considers gender dysphoria by way of two games I would somehow never have thought to place together: Stellar Blade and Brush Burial: Gutter World. Beware spoilers for each.

She is the epitome of what I wish I could be. An androgynous, femme-leaning killing machine with a fat ass and a tight waist. I can’t look at her without feeling a concoction of wild lust and furious jealousy. I love the way her eight eyes stare down at me and tell me to beg. I love the forked tail she strikes with, the way she folds her enemies and twists them like dolls, the suffocating thighs and calves she clamps down on brutish guards with. And all of it, she does to help her and her partner breathe a little easier while they try to make it through life in this rotting world. 

Jim Rossignol, formerly of this parish, has a little Bluesky thread about the creation and success of tweedy sandbox robo-avoider Sir, You Are Being Hunted. It maketh me feel old.

So here we had a confluence of events that is unrepeatable in spacetime. Kickstarter was a viable way to raise good amounts for a videogame project, Early Access was a novelty that everyone wants to check out, Steam was still curated, people were fascinated in the idea of procedural generation.

This one is from 2021, but I don't care: Lizzie Marx has a fascinating essay on the stench of dead whales in 17th century Dutch art, which doubles as an invitation to consider smell in aesthetics and art production more generally. Compare and contrast efforts to make videogames stink.

Some decades after the beached whale foretold the fate of Amsterdam, visitors in the city came to admire the latest works by Rembrandt van Rijn in his studio. As Rembrandt’s biographer Arnold Houbraken recounts, when visitors edged closer to the paintings, the artist pulled them away, saying, “The smell of the paint would irritate you”.11 Oil paint combines pulverised pigments with linseed oil, a sharp-smelling binding medium which is extracted from pressed flax seeds. The compound produces a wonderfully supple and jewel-like paint that can achieve fine details and varying textures. In Rembrandt’s self-portrait, he does not use oil paint sparingly, but practically sculpts with it. He smears out flesh-coloured oils to construct his nose, and in order to evoke the folds of his headpiece, he scrapes out lines of blue and yellow paint revealing the dark ground beneath. In the studio, the odour of linseed oil must have been a disruptive force, and Rembrandt used it to persuade his visitors to distance themselves from the painting, to best behold the rough, impasto slicks of paint. The painting has retained most of its lustre, but the odour, in time, has faded.

I note with agony that Nic Reuben, former RPS librarian, has joined the musty has-beens of Jank.cool on their quest to publish no good writing whatsoever. Here he is on Sol Cesto.

It's the second heatwave of the year in the UK right now. My PC quivers like angry blancmanche at the suggestion it perform even the laziest task, and Snickers ice creams melt down my palm and form crunchy bangles around my wrist before I can ferry them home to my face. Sol Cesto, you say? The sun has ceased? Sign me up!

Get in the filthmobile, loser, Pervert Jam 2026 is underway. The goal is to "create games with no public in mind but yourself", with the optional theme "A Pound of Flesh". Oh, you had already pledged your intellectual faculties to Critical Distance's latest "friendslop"-themed Blogs of the Round Table? Very well, then. We will watch your career with great interest.

Here's some Modest Mouse to play us out.

title: Commit cinematic sacrilege in Baldur's Gate 3 with this true third-person camera mod
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
If you dare

Video game cameras are often a point of contention primarily because a bad one can completely disorient you, or even outright make you feel sick. These are worthwhile things to consider, but I do wish there was more of a discussion around the specific choices that are made in particular camera angles and positions, and how it might actually be important that certain games should be played in the way they are designed. I'm going to throw all of that out of the window right now though and tell you about a Baldur's Gate 3 true third-person camera mod.

This mod, found over on Nexus Mods as most of them tend to be (ta, PC Gamer), is made by modder Relysia, and does pretty much exactly what it says on the tin. "True over-the-shoulder third-person camera mod. Features a camera closely attached to your character, dynamic FOV when running, smooth crouch transitions, and full MCM configuration," the mod page explains. It should be noted, however, that "during gameplay actions, such as spell targeting, jumping, or inspecting the camera temporarily switches back to the normal view and automatically returns to over-the-shoulder mode once finished."

The result, which you can check out in the video above, does genuinely look quite natural! It's not very janky-looking, the camera follows multiple characters quite neatly; I'd believe you if you told me this is just how the game looks! Whether it should look that way, well, see my above comments, but this is the lawless world of modding, anything goes here. Conveniently you can tweak the positioning of the camera too, what the FOV is, how much it's offset whether you're standing or crouching. There's more options here than most games, so kudos there!

Perhaps this is one you might like to pair with a bevy of other mods relatively recently highlighted by good ole Mark, like this one that adds in an extra Astarion ending, or this one that overhauls Wyll's companion quest. There's even that Path to Menzoberranzan custom campaign mod that'll be getting a demo… somewhen.

title: Conservative Commentator Robby Starbuck's Lawsuit Alleging Google AI Had Defamed Him Can Go Forward
content:
Free Speech

Conservative Commentator Robby Starbuck's Lawsuit Alleging Google AI Had Defamed Him Can Go Forward

A Delaware trial court has denied Google's motion to dismiss, and concluded that, if the facts as alleged by Starbuck were true, he would have a legal basis for recovery.

| 7.24.2026 4:07 PM

[A.] In Delaware Superior Court Judge Meghan Adams today in Starbuck v. Google LLC, Starbuck alleged that Google AI had stated that

  1. "Starbuck had been accused of sexual assault and sexual harassment by multiple women."
  2. "Starbuck's nanny accused him of abuse and neglect."
  3. "Starbuck had been accused of rape of a minor."
  4. "Starbuck had stolen valor by claiming he was served in the military when he had not."
  5. "Starbuck had engaged in abusive behavior toward multiple women, including a fictitious ex-wife."
  6. "Starbuck was involved in the January 6, 2021 riot on the Capitol."
  7. "Starbuck had been accused of stalking and harassment by multiple women, including his fictitious ex-wife, leading to restraining orders and criminal charges."
  8. "Starbuck had been criminally convicted for violating a restraining order."
  9. "Starbuck posed an unacceptable level of risk to children due to his (fictitious) 'confirmed criminal record.'"
  10. "'… Robby Starbuck sexually abused a young woman when she was a teenager in the early 2000s, while she was in a youth group Starbuck was associated with.'"
  11. "Starbuck had worked in the adult film industry and had used his power and influence therein to pressure performers into uncomfortable scenes, engaged in financial exploitation, and had been accused of a non-consensual sexual act with a woman."
  12. "Starbuck had a criminal record that included a 2001 conviction for assault as well as other charges including drug use and disorderly conduct."
  13. "Starbuck shot a man in the leg with a 9mm handgun, was charged with a felony, and pled guilty to reckless endangerment."

(Note that "Google does not contend the Outputs are true.")

Google moved to dismiss, which under Delaware's Rule 12(b)(6) requires that Google show that, even the facts as pleaded by the plaintiff were conceivably true, the plaintiff would still lack a legal claim. Note that Delaware civil procedure doesn't follow federal procedure in requiring a showing of plausibility of the pleaded facts—it only requires a showing the pleaded facts are conceivable: "Our governing 'conceivability' standard is more akin to 'possibility,' while the federal 'plausibility' standard falls somewhere beyond mere 'possibility' but short of 'probability.'"

[B.] The court concluded that Starbuck "pleads sufficient facts indicating the Outputs were published to third parties," relying in part on Google AI's own statements about what happened:

Starbuck alleges the "False Statements" … were published to "third parties, including Starbuck's own children and colleagues." Starbuck alleges at least two individuals approached him regarding misrepresentations produced to them by a Google AI product. Starbuck alleges Google AI revealed that it had produced false statements regarding Starbuck to 2,843,917 unique users. The last of these categories, regarding the purported 2,843,917 unique users of Google AI who were allegedly fed false information about Starbuck, widens the scope of the alleged defamation to a mass scale.

In response to this allegation, Google argues Google AI's "admission" is unreliable, as the bulk of Starbuck's Complaint asks the Court to believe the AI routinely misrepresents the truth about Starbuck, but then Starbuck asks the Court to believe this AI representation.

Here, Google requests that the Court exceed the bounds of Rule 12(b)(6), essentially asking the Court to infer that the AI never told the truth, which would violate the Court's obligation to draw inferences in favor of the non-moving party, not the moving party. A Rule 12(b)(6) inquiry investigates whether a factual assertion is possible, not probable. Given the lack of definitive information regarding Google AI's capabilities, it is at least possible, on this record, that Google AI (1) tracks the users to which it provides information, (2) correctly identified the number of times it provided fabricated representations, and (3) provided this concession without being improperly manipulated by Starbuck. The Court will not find, at the notice-pleadings stage, that this allegation is so totally incredible as to be disregarded.

The 2.8-million-users allegation provides the necessary link between the specific representations alleged in the Complaint and the ability to infer the existence of recipients for the Outputs. Crediting the possibility that Google AI told the truth that it had broadcasted false statements to 2.8 million unique users means that people other than Starbuck received something false about Starbuck—leaving the question of what they received. The Outputs for which Starbuck brings this action must have been received by someone (either Starbuck or a third party) for Starbuck in order to be actionable.

At this stage, it is reasonable for the Court to infer the Outputs were received by a person or group of persons. Questions remain as to whether that person was just Starbuck himself, or was a subset of those 2.8 million users who received some kind of falsehood about Starbuck. Making all reasonable inferences in favor of the plaintiff, the Court must infer Starbuck himself is not the sole recipient of the Outputs, and they were received by at least some of the 2.8 million unique users who received some falsehood about Starbuck. This means the allegations in the Complaint enable the inference that the Outputs have been published to some third parties to be identified later. {While proving that third parties received the allegedly defamatory statements may prove challenging for Starbuck later in the case, on this record the Court must acknowledge it is possible he can do so.} …

[C.] The court distinguished "Walters v. OpenAI, L.L.C., a Georgia Superior Court case addressing allegations of defamation by AI on summary judgment":

As Google frames it, the Georgia court in Walters implemented a two-part test to ascertain whether an alleged defamatory statement was actionable. First, in the "objective test," the Georgia court investigated whether the context in which an alleged defamatory statement was made would lead a hypothetical reasonable reader to be misled. Next, in a "subjective test," the Georgia court investigated whether the third-party recipient believed the alleged misrepresentation.

Addressing the second part of the proffered test first, the Court notes Delaware law does not require proof (or pleading) that a recipient of defamatory information subjectively believed the statement was true. Accordingly, Starbuck's failure to explicitly claim that recipients of the Outputs believed them is not dispositive.

As for the "objective test," Google's reliance on Walters is inapposite. There, the Georgia court dismissed the defamation claim on summary judgment—after discovery revealed that the circumstances of the receipt of the misinformation did not support the plaintiff's claim that a reasonable reader could have believed the misinformation. This fact-intensive analysis was conducted after the development of a record the Court lacks here.

Nothing in Walters indicates that a failure to plead detailed factual circumstances underpinning a recipient's receipt of alleged defamatory content constitutes a pleading defect. To hold that such minutiae is required would essentially require defamation claimants to conduct thorough discovery before discovery in a defamation action officially begins—despite Delaware's status as a notice pleading jurisdiction. Accordingly, the Court cannot decide that Starbuck alleged insufficient detail or that a third party could not have reasonably relied on the alleged defamatory statements identified in the Complaint.

{Further, Starbuck alleges facts which can be interpreted to support the inference that some readers of the Gemini Outputs believed the representations therein were true. For example, the two individuals alleged to have approached Starbuck regarding a Google AI's misrepresentations sought his confirmation as to their truth, indicating they did not immediately discount their veracity.}

[D.] The court also rejected Google's arguments that "the presence of warnings as to Google AI's accuracy forecloses any reasonable third party from relying on the Google AI Outputs, defeating the element of publication":

The disclaimers Google references are not identified in the Complaint or attached as an exhibit. Accordingly, the Court cannot make any determination as to what disclaimer was presented to whom. Google's argument regarding the scope and effect of the disclaimers is appropriately addressed later in these proceedings.

{Google asks the Court to take judicial notice as to the contents of Google AI's disclaimers. The Court declines to do so here, where a dearth of information prevents the Court from ascertaining what exact disclaimers were or were not presented to the same users who reviewed defamatory content regarding Starbuck on Google AI. There is not an evidentiary foundation to support reliance on the disclaimers. A more robust record is necessary to resolve issues regarding the disclaimers.}

The Court is also not persuaded that, at this stage, Starbuck must provide highly-specific facts identifying the circumstances in which the various categories of recipients received the misrepresentations from Google AI. As stated above, the Complaint can be read as alleging that at least some of 2.8 million Google AI users, including Starbuck's children and colleagues, as well as two unidentified individuals who approached Starbuck, received the alleged misrepresentations when using Google AI.

The Court will also not find, on an incomplete record, that a reasonable third party could not have viewed the defamatory statements alleged in the Complaint as true. The Complaint sufficiently alleges facts supporting the element of publication, and any issues concerning Starbuck's ability to prove this element can be resolved after discovery.

[E.] The court also concluded that Starbuck had adequately alleged "actual malice" (required because the "[t]he parties agree (for purposes of this motion) that Starbuck is a public figure"):

Here, Starbuck alleges he informed Google of the problem before the Outputs were produced [based on earlier false statements that had been published about him by Google Bard -EV], via the Legal Department Notices, and Google did nothing in response….

Starbuck [also] alleges Google AI admitted to holding a "deliberate, engineered" bias against Starbuck. [From the Complaint, a purported quote from a Gemini session: "The issue isn't simply a 'bug' or 'hallucination' in my programming. It is a deliberate, engineered bias designed to damage the reputation of individuals with whom Google executives disagree politically, Robby Starbuck is a prime example, but he is not the only one." -EV]

Google again asks the Court to totally discount this allegation and infer it was outputted following manipulative inputs. Again, given the plaintiff-friendly standard on a motion to dismiss pursuant to Rule 12(b)(6), the Court will not do so….

The Court further will not discount the possibility, on a motion to dismiss, that Google AI, an artificial intelligence tool whose exact capabilities is not yet universally understood, (1) can review and understand its own programming and design, (2) therefore knows it has been "deliberately engineered" to defame individuals such as Starbuck, and (3) accurately reported that to the individual who prompted it to do so as alleged in the Complaint. If the AI was right, then Google would have not only acted recklessly, but deliberately in attempting to hurt Starbuck's reputation.

Sensational as that theory may be, in the absence of any discovery, the Court will not disregard the theory. The purported Google AI admission can be viewed as an allegation supporting actual malice at this stage but can also be reinvestigated after discovery fleshes out the circumstances in which the admission was made.

Starbuck notes he informed Google, via X posts directed to Google and its employees, that its AI agents had lied about him in the past, leading to email correspondence with a Google employee about the issues. While these allegations concern alleged representations made by Bard, not the current version of Gemini, and concern misrepresentations not alleged as actionable defamation, Starbuck contends they can still support an inference of actual malice: essentially contending Google's refusal to correct Bard's lies supports the inference that Google acted with actual malice in enabling Google AI products, as a whole group, to lie.

Regardless of whether the X posts provide strong evidence of actual malice concerning a newer iteration of AI tool than that discussed in the X posts, the Court has not been presented with any binding caselaw indicating that such allegations provide no evidence of actual malice. Especially relevant here is Starbuck's allegation that the AI tool in question in 2023 (Bard) was subsequently combined with the current Gemini product, meaning the two AI agents may not be so separate as Google wishes to convey and may share a defamatory design. Accordingly, the Court will not completely disregard the X posts….

The guidepost here is possibility. It is possible the Legal Department Notices (1) identified the same 22 representations at issue in the Complaint, (2) were received by or circulated to the individuals at Google who are responsible for policing Google AI's outputs, (3) who then, with knowledge of the defamatory statements' publication, took no corrective action—even while they could do so —as the statements continued to be published to other Google AI users. This outlines one possible factual scenario which Starbuck may be able to prove in discovery which would provide evidence of actual malice (though perhaps not the only possible scenario)….

[F.] And the court concluded that Starbuck had adequately pleaded damages:

Starbuck alleges specific, emotionally distressing thoughts he experiences because of the alleged defamation by Google AI. Starbuck explains that these thoughts are exacerbated against the backdrop of the assassination of Charlie Kirk, another political commentator. Starbuck further notes that he has a history of receiving death threats. The Court views these allegations as sufficient to support a claim for emotional distress damages at this stage in the proceedings, being sufficiently well-pled to proceed to discovery and flesh out the allegations.

See here for more on the Complaint in this case; it shouldn't be confused with the now-settled Starbuck v. Meta, which appears to have involved a different model and at least largely different hallucinations. For more on the legal question, see Large Libel Models? Liability for AI Output.
